extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, social-science researchers, and methodological theorists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the proper scientific method for studying human nature, the formation of character (ethology), and social phenomena — emphasizing when to use deduction vs. observation and how to verify theoretical claims. Targets methodological standards for social-science inquiry and applied arts like education and politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of causal laws over empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The really scientific truths ... are the causal laws which explain [empirical laws].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical generalizations (observed regularities) serve chiefly to verify the conclusions of theory; true scientific knowledge consists in discovering the causal laws that explain those empirical regularities. When available, causal explanations determine the limits of applicability of empirical laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical laws are approximate and context-limited
rubrics_metrics.description: The empirical laws of those phenomena which depend on known causes ... are, even within the limits of observation, only approximate generalizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply empirical maxims far beyond the time, place, or circumstances in which they were observed. Examples/anti-patterns: assuming traits observed in one nationality, age group, or era will hold universally; transferring customs-derived maxims across different societies or generations without causal justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Deductive Method for very complex phenomena (Ethology)
rubrics_metrics.description: To such cases we have seen that the Deductive Method, setting out from general laws, and verifying their consequences by specific experience, is alone applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the formation of character and other highly complex phenomena, derive particular predictions by deducting from general laws of mind (psychology) rather than attempting direct experimental control of all variables. Deduction produces middle principles (ethological laws) to explain and predict tendencies in complex cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental/observational methods are limited for studying formation of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the laws of the formation of character susceptible of a satisfactory investigation by the method of experimentation? Evidently not ... a still more essential condition is wanting — the power of performing any of the experiments with scientific accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize practical impossibility of experimentally controlling or recording every influence in human upbringing. Observational studies must therefore be 'en masse' and comparative, not exhaustive, and will only yield approximate generalizations unless instances are numerous and diverse enough to eliminate chance and confounding circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle principles (axiomata media) are central to scientific value
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiomata media of every science principally constitute its value ... the middle principles should be arrived at ... and are the most valuable part of a science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to formulate and use intermediate (middle) principles that bridge high-level general laws and particular empirical laws. In social-science work, deriving these middle principles from general psychological laws provides the most practical and informative scientific knowledge for individual cases and policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification a posteriori must proceed pari passu with deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: It is hardly necessary again to repeat that ... verification a posteriori must proceed pari passu with deduction a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always test deductive predictions against empirical observations. The consilience (agreement) of a priori deduction and specific experience forms the sufficient ground for principles in complex sciences. Use empirical laws as checks and corrections on theoretical deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific propositions should assert tendencies, not certainties
rubrics_metrics.description: They must not assert that something will always, or certainly, happen; but only that such and such will be the effect of a given cause, so far as it operates uncounteracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame claims about human nature as tendencies (e.g., 'experience tends to give wisdom'), acknowledging possible frustrative influences. Avoid categorical universal claims when dealing with modifiable, context-sensitive phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed order of discovery; prioritize cases amenable to real induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The order in which truths of the various degrees of generality should be ascertained cannot ... be prescribed by any unbending rule. ... obtain those first in respect to which the conditions of a real induction can be first and most completely realized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the sequence of investigation pragmatically: begin with questions/cases where sufficient data and controllable conditions allow rigorous induction. Do not rigidly mandate lowest-to-highest generalizations if higher or middle principles are more accessible and informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simplest cases for inductive generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever our means of investigation can reach causes, without stopping at the empirical laws of the effects, the simplest cases, being those in which fewest causes are simultaneously concerned, will be most amenable to the inductive process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, limited-cause situations to establish broad causal laws. These simplest cases often yield the most comprehensive laws and serve as a firm basis for deducing more complex (middle) principles applicable elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define Ethology as the science of the formation of character
rubrics_metrics.description: A science is thus formed, to which I would propose to give the name of Ethology, or the Science of Character ... Ethology is the science which corresponds to the art of education in the widest sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ethology as a deductive discipline deriving how particular characters arise from general psychological laws plus sets of circumstances. Use it as the theoretical foundation for practical arts (education, policy) by translating principles into precepts adapted to individual circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect knowledge of tendencies can still be practically valuable
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be great power of influencing phenomena, with a very imperfect knowledge of the causes by which they are in any given instance determined. It is enough that we know that certain means have a tendency to produce a given effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In policy and education, apply knowledge of tendencies rather than waiting for perfect causal specification. Shape circumstances according to tendencies to produce desirable effects while recognizing limits of predictive certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical verification requires numerous and varied instances
rubrics_metrics.description: These conclusions ... deserve no reliance, even as such, unless the instances are sufficiently numerous to eliminate not only chance, but every assignable circumstance in which a number of the cases examined may happen to have resembled one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing empirical generalizations about human character or social types, ensure sample sizes and diversity large enough to exclude accidental patterns or shared confounders. Comparative statements (e.g., between nations) should be based on fair selection and sufficient counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Psychology (experimental) from Ethology (deductive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychology is altogether, or principally, a science of observation and experiment, Ethology ... is altogether deductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match method to subject-matter: use experimental/observational methods for discovering elementary psychological laws; use deduction from those laws to derive ethological/middle principles governing complex social and character-formation phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social phenomena conform to laws though prediction is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: All phenomena of society are phenomena of human nature, generated by the action of outward circumstances ... if the phenomena of human thought, feeling, and action are subject to fixed laws, the phenomena of society cannot but conform to fixed laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that, despite innumerable changing causes making long-term prediction impractical, social science can and should seek causal laws to explain current states, tendencies, and probable effects of interventions. The goal is explanation and guidance rather than absolute forecasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject purely Experimental/Chemical and purely Abstract/Geometrical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Two erroneous methods ... may be termed the Experimental, or Chemical, mode of investigation, and the Abstract, or Geometrical, mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying exclusively on either brute experiment without theoretical framing or on abstract universal precepts detached from empirical conditions. Prefer an approach that combines theoretical deduction with empirical verification and attention to particular circumstances.
